title: Install
text: Download the package for your system from the latest release. System Package Windows 10 or 11 (x64) genie-0.3.1-windows-x64-setup.exe macOS 11 or later (Apple silicon and Intel) genie-0.3.1-macos-universal.dmg Linux (x86_64) genie-0.3.1-linux-x86_64.AppImage or genie_0.3.1_amd64.deb The packages are not signed yet, so the system asks before genie opens the first time: Windows: if SmartScreen shows "Windows protected your PC", click More info, then Run anyway. The installer needs no administrator rights. It adds genie to the Start menu and opens .genie session files in genie. macOS: open the disk image and drag genie to Applications. Open genie. If macOS stops it, open System Settings > Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway. Linux: make the AppImage executable ( chmod +x genie-0.3.1-linux-x86_64.AppImage ) and run it. Some systems need FUSE 2 (the libfuse2 package). Or install the .deb with sudo apt install ./genie_0.3.1_amd64.deb . Each push to main also makes a test build for each operating system. The builds are in the artifacts of the CI runs for 30 days.

title: Build from source
text: Install rustup. rustup installs the toolchain version in rust-toolchain.toml . cargo run -p genie

title: Genomes
text: The start view lists ten genomes. Click a genome to open it with its gene track and its chromosome bands. Species Genome Assembly Gene track Human hg38 GRCh38 RefSeq Select Human hg19 GRCh37 RefSeq Select Human T2T T2T-CHM13v2.0 NCBI RefSeq Mouse mm39 GRCm39 RefSeq Select Mouse mm10 GRCm38 RefSeq Select Rat rn7 mRatBN7.2 NCBI RefSeq Zebrafish danRer11 GRCz11 NCBI RefSeq Fly dm6 BDGP6 NCBI RefSeq Worm ce11 WBcel235 NCBI RefSeq Yeast sacCer3 R64 NCBI RefSeq genie gets the genome files from the UCSC Genome Browser download server. It reads the sequence over the web, as for other files on the web. RefSeq Select has one transcript for each gene. NCBI RefSeq has all transcripts. Type a gene name, for example BRCA1, in the locus box to go to the gene. The overview strip shows the chromosome bands. Put the pointer on a band to see its name. If a genome has no band data, the strip is a plain bar. genie uses the contig names of the genome. A track that uses 1 , NC_000001.11 or CM000663.2 shows on chr1 of hg38. The label left of the locus box shows the open genome. Click the label to open a different genome or a reference file. genie keeps the small genome files (contig names, bands and genes) in its cache folder. It gets them again after 30 days. To use a genome without a network connection, click the genome label, then click Use offline. genie downloads the full sequence into its cache folder (human: about 835 MB). If the download stops, genie continues it the next time. Click Remove offline copy to delete the sequence. If the open genome reads from the offline copy, genie first changes it to the sequence on UCSC. Sessions and the recent list keep the genome.

title: NCBI assemblies
text: UCSC GenArk has assembly hubs for thousands of NCBI assemblies of other species. To open one, click Other NCBI assemblies… in the start view, or click the genome label and then NCBI assembly…. The palette has Open an NCBI assembly… too. Type a species, a common name or an accession, for example Gallus gallus , chicken or GCF_016699485.2 . The list shows the assemblies that have all the words. Accessions that start with the words come first, then species and common names that start with them. Outdated assemblies, which UCSC keeps in its legacy set, come after the others and show outdated. Click an assembly. genie opens its GenArk hub, then the genome of the hub. The hub dialog then shows the tracks of the hub, such as the genes of NCBI RefSeq. An accession with its version (GCA or GCF, nine digits, a dot and the version) also opens from Open URL… and Open a track hub…, and from the dialog when it is not in the list. genie gets the list of GenArk assemblies (about 6 MB) from UCSC the first time you open the dialog, and keeps it in its cache folder for 7 days. Without a network connection, genie uses the list that it has. The contigs of a GenArk genome have the names in its 2bit file, often the NCBI accessions of the sequences.

title: UCSC tracks
text: Click the tracks button (the layers icon) in the title bar to add a public track from the UCSC Genome Browser to the open genome. Genome Genes Variation Conservation Regulation hg38 MANE Select, GENCODE V48 ClinVar, dbSNP 155 common phyloP 100-way, phastCons 100-way, GC percent ENCODE cCREs hg19 GENCODE V48lift37 ClinVar, dbSNP 155 common phyloP 100-way, phastCons 100-way mm39 GENCODE VM37 EVA SNP 6 phyloP 35-way, phastCons 35-way, GC percent mm10 UCSC Genes EVA SNP 6 phyloP 60-way, phastCons 60-way, GC percent ENCODE cCREs T2T, rn7, danRer11 GC percent dm6 phyloP 124-way, GC percent ce11 phyloP 135-way, GC percent genie reads these tracks in parts from the UCSC download server, as for other files on the web. The track gets the name from the list, for example ClinVar. A track that is open shows Added in the list. For yeast and for reference files, the menu has no UCSC tracks. It always has the track hubs. Sessions keep these tracks with their names.

title: Track hubs
text: A track hub is a set of track files on a web server, with a hub.txt file that names them. The UCSC Genome Browser uses track hubs. To open a track hub: 1. Click the tracks button, then click Open a track hub…. The genie menu and the palette (Ctrl+K) also have this item. 2. Type the address of the hub.txt file, then push Enter. A dialog shows the tracks of the hub for the open genome, in their groups: super tracks, composite tracks and views. Type words to find a track. Click a track to add it. Click it again to remove it. Open URL (Ctrl+U) also opens a hub when the address ends with .txt . To open a hub on your computer, open its hub.txt file. genie reads the hub, genomes and trackDb files of the hub, and the files that their include lines name. It uses the genome of the hub that has the name of the open genome, for example hg38, or the name of the reference file. genie adds tracks of these types: bigBed, bigWig and the other UCSC big formats (for example bigGenePred and bigNarrowPeak), bam, cram, vcfTabix and hic. genie uses the type and the index that the hub gives, so the file names can be anything. The list shows tracks of other types, for example longTabix, but genie cannot add them. A track gets its short label from the hub as its name. If the hub has no tracks for the open genome, the dialog lists the genomes of the hub. Click a genome to open it with the tracks of the hub. genie opens the 2bit sequence of an assembly hub, or the UCSC genome with the same name. The dialog shows the first 500 rows. Type words to find the other tracks. The tracks button lists the hubs of the session and the 8 hubs that you opened last. Sessions keep their hubs, and the type and the index of each track from a hub.

title: Files
text: Kind Formats Reference sequence FASTA ( .fa , .fasta , .fna , .fas ), FASTA compressed with bgzip ( .fa.gz ), UCSC 2bit ( .2bit ) Feature track BED, GFF3 and GTF (plain, gzip or bgzip); bigBed ( .bb ) Alignment track BAM; CRAM 3.0 and 3.1; PAF from minimap2, wfmash and other aligners ( .paf ); PSL from BLAT ( .psl ). PAF and PSL are plain, gzip or bgzip Variant track VCF (plain, gzip or bgzip); BCF ( .bcf ) with its CSI index ( .bcf.csi ) Signal track bigWig ( .bw ); bedGraph (plain, gzip or bgzip); bedMethyl from modkit (plain, gzip or bgzip) Interaction track bigInteract ( .bb ); BEDPE ( .bedpe , plain or gzip, up to 50 MB); loop lists of Juicer and HiCCUPS ( .txt , plain or gzip) Junction track STAR splice junctions ( SJ.out.tab ); junction BED files of TopHat and regtools ( junctions.bed , or a BED file with the track line track name=junctions or graphType=junctions ). Plain or gzip, up to 50 MB Hi-C track Juicer .hic , versions 6 to 9; cooler .cool and .mcool , as from the 4D Nucleome project Table track Tab-separated tables compressed with bgzip and indexed with tabix -s -b -e , for example the CADD scores ( .tsv.gz , .txt.gz and others, with .tbi or .csi ) GWAS track Summary statistics of the GWAS Catalog, PLINK 2 ( .glm.linear , .glm.logistic ), REGENIE ( .regenie ), SAIGE and BOLT-LMM: tab or space separated, plain or gzip up to 1 GB, or bgzip with a tabix index Copy number track SEG ( .seg , as from TCGA, DNAcopy or GISTIC); CNVkit ( .cns , .cnr ); GATK ModelSegments ( .seg ). Plain or gzip, up to 50 MB Sample table Tab or comma separated text with a header line ( .tsv , .csv , .txt , .panel from the 1000 Genomes Project); clinical files from cBioPortal; IGV sample information files; PLINK .fam and .ped . Plain or gzip, up to 64 MB Session genie session ( .genie ) Open a genome or a reference sequence first. Then open tracks or drop them on the window. If a FASTA file has no index ( .fai , and .gzi for bgzip), genie makes the index and keeps it in its cache folder. For a large file, this can take some seconds. To make the indexes before you open the file: bgzip genome.fa && samtools faidx genome.fa.gz

title: Files without an index
text: If a track file has an index next to it ( .tbi , .csi , .bai or .crai ), genie uses that index. If the file has no index, genie prepares the file in its cache folder: A sorted BAM file, a CRAM file or a sorted bgzip file gets an index. genie does not copy the file. A BCF file without its CSI index opens if it is 50 MB or less: genie reads all of it. Index larger BCF files with bcftools index . A plain or gzip file gets a copy compressed with bgzip, and an index. Plain files up to 50 MB open directly, without a copy. A file that is not sorted by position gets a sorted copy, for example a GTF file from GENCODE or Ensembl, or a BAM file from an aligner. genie sorts on disk, so the size of the file is not limited by memory. While genie prepares a file, the track shows the step and the progress, for example "Sorting genes.gtf.gz… 45 %". The track shows its data when the work is complete. To stop the work, click × on the track. genie keeps the copies and indexes until you clear them. The settings panel shows the space that they use. Click Clear to remove them. genie keeps the files of open tracks. If a track file changes, genie prepares it again. You can also prepare files yourself, for example to use them in other programs. To prepare a BED track: sort -k1,1 -k2,2n genes.bed bgzip > genes.bed.gz && tabix -p bed genes.bed.gz For GFF3 and GTF, sort by columns 1 and 4 and use tabix -p gff : sort -k1,1 -k4,4n genes.gtf bgzip > genes.gtf.gz && tabix -p gff genes.gtf.gz genie shows features when the view is 10 Mb or less. Wider views show the density of the features: bigBed files from their zoom levels, other files as the number of features per Mb. For a file with a tabix or CSI index, genie estimates the density from the index, without reading the features. This needs an index from htslib (tabix, bcftools or samtools), which counts the records of each contig. To prepare a BAM track: samtools sort -o reads.bam reads.sam && samtools index reads.bam A CRAM file keeps the bases of a read as differences from a reference. genie uses the reference that is open, so open the genome or the FASTA file that made the CRAM file. Each part of a CRAM file has the MD5 of its reference bases. If the open reference is different there, the track says "The reference is not the reference of the CRAM file here." and does not show wrong bases. CRAM files that hold their own reference, or that do not need one, open with any reference. genie reads CRAM 3.0 and 3.1 files with gzip, rANS and rANS Nx16 compression. This is what most archives and samtools make by default. genie does not read the arithmetic coder, fqzcomp and the name tokenizer of CRAM 3.1, and bzip2 and lzma blocks. The small and archive profiles of samtools use them. genie shows reads when the view is 30 kb or less. It hides QC-fail and secondary reads. By default, it also hides duplicate reads and soft clips, and it keeps 100 reads for each 50 bp. To prepare a large VCF track: bgzip calls.vcf && tabix -p vcf calls.vcf.gz genie shows variants when the view is 1 Mb or less. Wider views show the number of variants per Mb, estimated from the index as for feature files. Put the pointer on the bars to see the density, for example "About 520 variants per Mb". To prepare a large bedGraph track: sort -k1,1 -k2,2n signal.bedGraph bgzip > signal.bedGraph.gz && tabix -p bed signal.bedGraph.gz genie shows bigWig tracks and plain bedGraph tracks at all zoom levels. It shows a bedGraph track that has a tabix index when the view is 10 Mb or less. For the best speed, convert bedGraph to bigWig with bedGraphToBigWig. A bedMethyl file from modkit pileup is a BED file. To prepare a large bedMethyl track: sort -k1,1 -k2,2n calls.bed bgzip > calls.bedMethyl.gz && tabix -p bed calls.bedMethyl.gz genie shows a bedMethyl track that has a tabix index when the view is 10 Mb or less.

title: PAF alignments
text: A PAF file from minimap2, wfmash or another aligner shows each alignment on its target sequence, as a feature with the name of the query. So make the PAF file with the reference in view as the target, for example minimap2 -cx asm5 genome.fa other.fa > other.paf . If a line has a CIGAR (the cg tag, from minimap2 -c ), each deletion of 50 bases or more from the target splits the alignment into blocks with a thin line between them, as the exons of a transcript. The card shows the place on the query, for example contig_7:1001-4100 , the identity (matches / alignment block length), the matches, the block length, MAPQ and the short tags, such as the type (primary, secondary or inversion), the edits (NM) and the divergence (dv). Filters work on these fields, for example Identity (%) at least 95 or Type primary. Type a query name in the locus box to go to its alignment. A plain PAF file up to 50 MB opens directly. genie sorts and indexes larger files in its cache. To prepare a PAF file yourself: sort -k6,6 -k8,8n other.paf bgzip > other.paf.gz && tabix -0 -s6 -b8 -e9 other.paf.gz

title: Files on the web
text: genie can open reference sequences and tracks from a web server. To open a file from the web: 1. Push Ctrl+U (Cmd+U on macOS) or click the link button. 2. Type the address of the file. The address must start with https:// , http:// , s3:// or gs:// . 3. Push Enter. You can also give addresses as arguments: cargo run -p genie -- https://example.org/data/genome.2bit https://example.org/data/reads.bam genie reads only the parts of a file that the view needs. The server must send parts of files (HTTP range requests). If the server sends only full files, genie opens only files of 4 MB or less. genie looks for the index on the same server. The address of an index is the address of the file with the index extension, for example reads.bam.bai . If a track file on the web has no index, genie downloads the file into its cache folder and prepares it there, as for files on your computer. The limit is 1 GB. If you stop a download, it continues from where it stopped the next time that you open the file. genie does not make indexes for FASTA files from the web. genie reads plain BED, GFF3, GTF, VCF, bedGraph and bedMethyl files up to 50 MB completely. For files that genie reads from the web in parts, the locus box finds names only in bigBed files that have a name index. genie keeps up to 64 MB of data from the web in memory. It writes a file from the web to disk only when it must make an index for the file. genie opens files in public buckets of Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage, for example s3://1000genomes/phase3/data/HG00096/alignment/HG00096.chrom20.ILLUMINA.bwa.GBR.low_coverage.20120522.bam or gs://gcp-public-data--gnomad/release/4.1/vcf/genomes/gnomad.genomes.v4.1.sites.chr21.vcf.bgz . genie reads them through the HTTPS addresses of the buckets. It does not sign requests, so it cannot open private buckets or Requester Pays buckets. genie uses the certificates of the operating system for HTTPS. A connection to an http:// address is not secure. genie does not send user names, passwords or cookies. Sessions and the recent list keep the addresses of files from the web. genie cannot open a session file from the web.

title: Navigation
text: Drag the tracks to move along the sequence. Turn the wheel with Ctrl (Cmd on macOS) to zoom. Push the arrow keys to move and + or - to zoom. The buttons right of the locus box zoom out, zoom in, show the whole chromosome and show the whole genome. Click the genie logo for a menu with the main actions and their keys. Push Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on macOS) to find an action by its words, for example "group phase", then push Enter. Push F1 or click the ? button to see all keys and mouse actions. In a narrow window, the title bar hides the buttons that the genie menu also has: save, export, help, settings and the whole genome. Then the other buttons and the locus box stay in the window. Drag on the ruler to zoom to that range. Push Escape to stop the drag. To go back to an earlier view, push Alt+Left (Cmd+[ on macOS), push the back button of the mouse or click the back arrow left of the locus box. Alt+Right (Cmd+] on macOS) goes forward again. genie keeps the last 100 jumps: the locus box, name search, ruler drags, region and feature jumps and changes of contig. Moves and zooms do not add a step. Push Ctrl+F or Ctrl+B (Cmd on macOS) to go to the next or the previous feature or variant of the track under the pointer. The search continues on the next contigs. The track menu has the same items. genie sorts the contigs. First are the numbered chromosomes in number order (1, 2 … 22, also arms such as 2L and 2R, and Roman numbers such as I to XVI). Then come X, Y, W and Z, and then M. The other contigs follow in the order of the file. The region list and the feature search use this order.

title: Find a sequence
text: Push Ctrl+Shift+F (Cmd+Shift+F on macOS), or click Find a sequence… in the logo menu or the palette. A find bar opens under the ruler. Type the bases, for example a primer. You can use the IUPAC codes, for example N, R and Y. genie ignores spaces, digits and the marks in 5'-…-3' . The sequence can have 2 to 200 bases. genie finds the bases on the two strands. A lane under the find bar shows a bar for each match in the view, with arrows for its strand. A sequence that is the same on the two strands, such as GAATTC , shows one bar without arrows. Click 1, 2 or 3 next to Mismatches to also find near matches. Near matches have a light color, and when you zoom in, the wrong bases have a vermillion mark. Each mismatch needs 4 bases in the sequence, for example 8 bases for 2 mismatches. Unknown bases (N) in the reference do not match. Push Enter to go to the next match, and Shift+Enter to go to the previous match. If there is no match near the view, genie reads 20 Mb of the reference each time that you push Enter. At the end of a chromosome, it continues on the next chromosome. Put the pointer on a match to see its locus, its strand, its mismatches and its bases as they read on its strand. Wrong bases are lower case. Click to keep the card open. genie finds sequences when the view is 10 Mb or less, and shows up to 100,000 matches. Push Escape or click × to close the find bar.

title: Primer pairs
text: Click Primers in the find bar to find the PCR products of a primer pair, as an in-silico PCR. Type the forward primer and the reverse primer, each from its 5′ end to its 3′ end. Each primer needs 12 bases or more. A product starts at the forward primer on one strand and ends at the reverse primer on the other strand. genie finds the products on the two strands of the reference, up to 4,000 bp long. In the lane, a product is a line with a block for each primer and arrows for its strand. Mismatches allows 1, 2 or 3 wrong bases in each primer. The 5 bases at the 3′ end of each primer must match, because the polymerase extends from there. Push Enter and Shift+Enter to go to the next and the previous product. Put the pointer on a product to see its locus, its length, its strand, its mismatches and its primers. Click Bases to find one sequence again.

title: BLAT
text: The BLAT server of UCSC finds where a sequence aligns in the whole genome, also with gaps and introns. genie can send a sequence to it when the open genome is a genome of UCSC, such as hg38 or mm39. Click BLAT a sequence… in the palette, type or paste the bases (plain or FASTA, 20 to 8,000 bases), then push Enter or click BLAT. To BLAT a read, click the read to keep its card open, then click BLAT in the card. If the read has a soft clip of 20 bases or more, Use the clipped part puts the longest clip in the box, for example to find where the clipped part of a split read comes from. UCSC takes BLAT searches from programs only with the API key of a person. To make your key, log in to your account at genome.ucsc.edu, open the Hub Development page and make a key in its API key part. Paste the key in UCSC API key in the dialog. genie keeps the key in its settings file on this computer and does not show it in messages. Without a key, Search on the UCSC page opens the same search in your web browser. genie also opens PSL files that you save from UCSC. genie sends only the bases and your key to UCSC. UCSC asks for at most one search each 15 seconds, so genie waits that long between two searches. The dialog lists the alignments, the best score first, with the locus, the strand, the identity, the score and the length. Click an alignment to go there. genie keeps the alignments as a PSL file in its cache folder and opens it as a track, named "BLAT" and the name of the sequence. The track shows each alignment with its blocks, and Ctrl+F and Ctrl+B go to the next and the previous alignment. The card of an alignment shows the place on the query, the identity, the score, the matches, the mismatches and the gaps. genie opens other PSL files too, for example from BLAT on the command line. Index a large PSL file without its header with tabix -0 -s14 -b16 -e17 , or let genie prepare it in its cache.

title: Several loci
text: Type two to four loci in the locus box, with a space between them, for example BRCA1 BRCA2 . genie shows the loci side by side in panels of equal width. The top of each panel shows its locus and its ruler. Click the locus to show only that panel. Click × to close the panel. To show one panel again, type one locus. Drag, turn the wheel or drag on the ruler in a panel to move or zoom that panel. The arrow keys and + and - move and zoom all panels. Put the pointer on a feature, a read or a variant in a panel to see its data. Back, forward, region jumps and feature jumps move the first panel. Sessions, Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on macOS) and the goto command keep all loci. Images show all panels.

title: Whole genome
text: Type All (or genome ) in the locus box, or click the button with four bars right of the zoom buttons, to see all main chromosomes side by side. The genie menu and the palette also have Show the whole genome. Each chromosome is as wide as its share of the genome, and at least 3 pixels wide. The ruler shows the names of the chromosomes that have space, without "chr". genie does not show alt, random, unplaced and patch contigs (names with _ ). If a reference has more than 50 contigs, genie shows the 50 longest. Tracks show what they show for a whole chromosome: signal tracks show their bars, copy number tracks show their rows, and feature and variant tracks show their density. All chromosomes use one scale, and the range shows once at the right of the track. Read tracks and other tracks that need a closer view show one hint. Click a chromosome on the ruler or on a track to show it. Drag across a part of a chromosome to show that region. Put the pointer on the data to see its card. Back and forward return to the whole-genome view. Sessions keep it.

title: Regions
text: Click the bookmark button to show the region list. Push Ctrl+D (Cmd+D on macOS) to add the view to the list, or hold Shift and drag on the ruler to add a range. Click a region to go to it. Double-click a region to change its name, then push Enter. Import BED and Export BED read and write the list as a BED file. genie reads plain BED files up to 50 MB. It does not import regions on contigs that are not in the reference. Lift… moves the regions from a different assembly to the assembly in view with a chain file (see Liftover). Regions show as bands under the ruler. Put the pointer on a band to see its name, and click the band to go to the region.

title: Copy
text: Push Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on macOS) to copy the locus of the view, for example chr1:1,001-2,000 . If the view has several loci, genie copies all of them, with a space between them. If you clicked a card to keep it open, Ctrl+C copies the text of the card. Right-click the ruler or a region in the region list, then click Copy locus or Copy sequence. Copy sequence copies the bases in FASTA format, with 60 bases on each line. The header is the locus, for example >chr1:1001-2000 . If the sequence track shows the reverse strand, genie copies the reverse complement and adds (-) to the header. genie copies up to 1 Mb.

title: Tracks
text: Put the pointer on a feature, a read or a variant to see its data. Click to keep the card open. A card also shows the other fields of the file: bigBed fields with the descriptions from the file, GFF3 and GTF attributes, and the BED columns after column 12 (Column 13 and so on). A variant card shows the INFO entries with the descriptions from the ##INFO lines of the header. If two descriptions give the same short label, the card shows the INFO IDs, for example AF_EUR and AF_EUR_unrel . genie does not show empty fields, fields with the value none or . , and bigBed fields that UCSC hides (names that start with _ ). In a bigBed card, each item of a list keeps its place, and an item without a value (empty, -inf or nan ) shows as –. For example, the alleles and the frequencies of the projects in dbSNP agree item by item. A Sequence Ontology number shows its term, for example 5_prime_UTR_variant (SO:0001623) . genie does not show 0, which is no term. A card shows up to 6 fields. Click to keep the card open and see all fields. If the card is taller than the window, scroll it. Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on macOS) copies the card with all fields. genie keeps the first 400 characters of the INFO column of each variant, without the annotations of VEP, SnpEff and bcftools (see below). If it cuts the INFO column, the card shows More INFO. A variant card shows QUAL and FILTER as the fields Quality and Filter. A variant card also shows the change of the variant on the transcripts of the open feature tracks, in HGVS notation, for example "BRCA1 p.Arg1699Trp · c.5095C>T". genie uses the transcripts in view that have a strand and a coding part, for example from BED12, bigBed, GFF3 and GTF files, and gets the bases from the reference. The card shows up to 3 transcripts, with the protein changes first, and the number of the other transcripts. "p.Leu12=" keeps the amino acid, "p.Arg37Ter" makes a stop codon and "p.Lys45fs" moves the reading frame. A variant in the 2 bases next to an exon shows "splice site". A variant out of the coding sequence shows its place and its c. position: 5′ UTR (for example "c.-14G>A"), 3′ UTR ("c.*32C>T") or intron ("c.92+5G>A"). A deletion of whole exons shows "exon deletion", and a deletion of the whole transcript shows "transcript deletion". A change of the stop codon shows the extension, for example "p.Ter148GluextTer?". An allele with unknown bases (N) shows "p.?". As HGVS asks, genie moves an insertion or a deletion in a repeat to the 3′ end of the transcript, and an insertion of the bases before it is a duplication, for example "c.417dup" or "p.Lys2dup". Each alternate allele of a site has its own lines. genie does not use a transcript if the length of its coding part is not a multiple of 3. If the VCF file has annotations from Ensembl VEP ( CSQ ), SnpEff ( ANN ) or bcftools csq ( BCSQ ), the variant card shows the 3 most severe annotations, one line for each, for example "BRCA1 · missense_variant · MODERATE · ENST00000357654.9:c.5095C>T · p.Arg1699Trp", and the number of the other annotations. For the same impact, the transcripts that VEP marks as canonical, MANE Select or picked come first. bcftools csq does not give the impact, so genie gets it from the consequence, as VEP does. The fields Consequence, Impact, Gene and Biotype list the values of all annotations of the variant. Use them to filter the track, for example to keep only the variants with a HIGH impact. The other columns of the first annotation are fields with the name of the INFO field before them, for example CSQ SIFT . genie finds annotations in each INFO field whose description names its columns, as VEP, SnpEff and bcftools write them. To filter a track, click a value in a card that you keep open. Then click Keep only or Hide the value. For a number, the menu has a box with the value: keep it or type a different number, then click At least or At most. Each rule hides more features or variants. A value with commas passes when one of its items passes, for example the tags of a GENCODE transcript or the frequencies of a dbSNP variant. A filtered track shows the number of features or variants in view that it keeps, for example "12 of 586", at the top right. Click the number, or right-click the track, to see the rules. Click × to remove a rule. Click Label with this field in the same menu to name the features with that field, for example the gene type. Label with name in the track menu goes back. Filters and labels apply when the track shows features or variants. A filtered bigBed track wider than 10 Mb shows the density of the features that the filter keeps, if their data in view is 16 MB or less. If there is more data, the track shows the density of all features, and the count asks you to zoom in. Next feature and Previous feature skip the features and variants that the filter hides. If you type a name that a filter hides, genie goes to it and a note says so, for example "TP53 is hidden by the filter of GENCODE V48." Sessions and images keep the filters. Type a feature name or a variant ID in the locus box to go to it. The search ignores letter case. genie finds variant IDs in VCF files up to 50 MB. It also finds names in bigBed files that have a name index ( bedToBigBed -extraIndex=name ), and in other bigBed files up to 50 MB. BED and bigBed features use the colors of the file (itemRgb). Right-click the track and turn off "Use file colors" to use the track color. In a bigBed file of gene models (bigGenePred), each transcript shows its gene symbol. genie uses the field that the file describes as the gene symbol. If there is no such field, it uses geneName2 , then name2 . A track from the UCSC track list can set the field. For example, mm10 UCSC Genes uses geneName . In a variant track, the color of a site shows the change: the color of the new base for an SNV, purple for an insertion and dark grey for a deletion. A site that does not pass FILTER has a light color. Structural variants from callers such as Sniffles2, Manta, DELLY, pbsv and cuteSV show over their full length: a deletion in dark grey, a duplication in vermillion, an inversion in green and an insertion in purple. genie finds them by their SVTYPE, by a symbolic allele such as <DEL> or <DUP:TANDEM> , or by a breakend such as G]chr17:198982] . The card says the type and the length, for example "Deletion · 2,345 bp", and "imprecise" for an IMPRECISE call. A complex rearrangement, such as a CPX record of gnomAD-SV, also shows over its full length, and its card says "Complex rearrangement". Thin lines with ends show the confidence intervals of the start and the end (CIPOS and CIEND). A lane above the sites shows each breakend (BND) as an arc to its other end. Two breakends that join each other give one arc. A breakend to another chromosome shows as a stub, and its card names the other end, for example "Breakend · other end chr2:321,682". genie finds the other end in the alternate allele, or in CHR2 with POS2, END2 or END, as gnomAD-SV and other callers write it. A breakend takes one base, also when its END is on the other side. Under the sites, each sample has a row: a light color for heterozygous, the full color for homozygous alternate and grey for homozygous reference. A sample with no call has no mark. If there are more than 100 samples, the rows are thin. If there are more than 300 samples, each row shows a group of samples with the strongest call of the group (homozygous alternate, then heterozygous, then homozygous reference), and the card names the samples of the row. A signal track has a bar for each pixel. The bar goes to the mean value, and a light color goes to the maximum value. Values below zero go down from a zero line. The range of the values in view is at the top right. Right-click a signal track to show a line instead of bars. Turn on "Shared scale" on two or more signal tracks to give them the same range. To fix the range of a signal track, right-click it, type the minimum and the maximum, then push Enter. The fields show the range in view. Auto range goes back to the range of the data in view. A track with a fixed range does not use "Shared scale". To show two or more signal tracks in one lane, right-click a signal track, then click a track under Overlay on. The lane shows each signal as a line in the color of its track, with one range for all. If two tracks have the same color, genie gives the added track a different color. To show a track in its own lane again, right-click the lane and click the track under Separate. To compare a signal track with another signal track, for example ChIP with its input, right-click the track and click the other track under Compare with. The lane then shows the log2 ratio of the two values at each pixel, with 1 added to each value, so that a value of 0 does not give an infinite ratio. Right-click the lane to show the Ratio or the Difference instead, or click Stop comparing. A chip at the right of the lane names the comparison, and the card shows its value. The lane shows nothing where the other track has no value. If you remove the other track, the comparison stops. Sessions keep the comparisons. Double-click a track name to change it, then push Enter. Push Escape to stop. If you delete the name, the track shows its file name again. The track menu also has Rename. Right-click a track to set its rows, its color or its place. When the pointer is on a track, a ⋯ button next to its name opens the same menu and a × button removes the track. Click Track settings… at the top of the track menu to see all settings of the track in one dialog: name, color, rows, height, and the settings of its kind. Each change shows at once. Right-click a read track to show duplicate reads and soft clips, or to keep all reads. genie colors unusual read pairs: vermillion for an insert size that is larger than expected, blue for a smaller one, green for two mates on the same strand, purple for mates that point away from each other, and orange for a mate on a different chromosome. The expected insert sizes come from the loaded pairs. Right-click a read track to turn these colors off. Right-click a read track and click View as pairs to put the two mates of each pair on one row, with a thin line between them. A pair takes the space from the start of one mate to the end of the other, so pairs with an unusual insert size are easy to see. A mate whose other mate is not in the loaded region stays alone, and secondary and supplementary reads do not join a pair. An insertion in a read has a purple mark when you zoom in to single bases. An insertion of 10 bases or more, as long reads often have, has a purple box with its length in every view, and a mark in squished and collapsed rows. Put the pointer on the mark or the box: the read card shows the length and the place of the insertion, and the field Inserted bases holds its bases. Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on macOS) copies the card with all the bases. Right-click a read track to sort the rows by the base at that position, or to group the reads by phase (HP tag) or by strand. The card of a paired read shows the mate position, the insert size, the pair orientation and the HP and RG tags. A read card also lists MAPQ, the insert size of a pair and the small tags of the read as fields, for example NM, AS or CB. In a card that you keep open, click a field to keep only or hide the reads with that value, or to keep the reads with at least or at most a number. genie loads the reads again with the filter. For a tag, the menu also has Group by this tag and Color by this tag. Groups show numbers in order, then text values, then the reads without the tag. A track shows at most 30 groups: the smallest ones go together as "Other values". Color by a tag gives the 5 most common values in the loaded reads the 5 track colors. The other reads are grey. Right-click the track and click Group by or Color by with the tag name to stop. CRAM files from samtools usually leave out the NM and MD tags, so their reads do not show them. Right-click a read track to show secondary reads, supplementary reads or reads that failed the quality checks of the sequencer, and to hide the reads under MAPQ 1, 10, 20 or 30 (MAPQ ≥). Sessions keep these settings. A read with MAPQ 0 is placed in more than one spot of the genome. genie shows it in a light color, and its card says "placed in more than one spot". A split read has other parts in the genome (SA tag). A dark mark shows the clipped end of the read. The card lists the other parts, for example "chr2:1,234,000 + · MAPQ 60". In a card that you keep open, click a part to go to it. A read that spans an intron (N in the CIGAR) shows a thin line over the intron. Above the reads, an arc joins the two ends of each splice junction. A higher and thicker arc has more reads. The color of the arc shows the strand: blue for forward, vermillion for reverse and grey if the strand is not known. The strand comes from the XS or ts tag of the reads. If the reads have no such tag, it comes from the bases at the two ends of the intron: GT-AG, GC-AG or AT-AC on the forward strand, or their reverse complements. If there is space, the arc shows its number of reads. The count includes all reads, also the reads that down-sampling hides. Put the pointer on an arc to see its position, reads, strand and intron length. A collapsed read track shows the coverage and the arcs. Long reads can have base modifications (MM and ML tags), for example 5mC from nanopore or PacBio. Right-click a read track and turn on Color by modification. The reads become grey, and each call has a color: vermillion for modified, blue for not modified, and a light color for a probability near 50%. Mismatches stay on top. When you zoom out, a pixel shows the mean probability of its calls. The card of a read counts the calls for each modification, for example "Modified 5mC 34 of 120" (calls with a probability of 50% or more). When Color by modification is on, a lane above the reads shows the share of modified reads at each site. A vermillion bar goes up to the share of modified calls, and grey fills the rest. If you group the reads by phase or by strand, each group has a lane with the group name. At a CpG, genie adds the calls of the two strands together, at the C of the forward strand. Put the pointer on a bar to see the counts, for example "Modified 12 of 20 reads · 60 %", and the counts of the other modifications at the site. The lane shows 5mC, or the modification with the most calls if the reads have no 5mC. To show a different modification, right-click the track and click it, for example Show 5hmC. genie opens bedMethyl files from modkit pileup as signal tracks. genie knows a bedMethyl file by its name ( .bedMethyl , also compressed) or by its columns, also if the name ends with .bed . The bars show the percent of modified reads, from 0 to 100. Right-click the track to select the modification, for example Show 5hmC. Join CpG strands adds the counts of the two strands of each CpG together, at the C of the forward strand. genie joins two sites only if the file has a site on each strand. Turn it off to see each strand. Zoom in until a pixel shows less than 8 bp: then the card of a site shows its counts, for example "Modified 12 of 20 reads · 60 %". An interaction track shows links between two regions, for example chromatin loops from Hi-C or ChIA-PET. genie opens bigInteract files (bigBed files with the UCSC interact fields, also with the older names region1 and region2 of the ends), BEDPE files, and the loop lists of Juicer and HiCCUPS. In a loop list, the header line gives the names of all fields, and the color column gives the color of each arc. Each link is an arc from the middle of one end to the middle of the other, with a small block at each end. A longer link rises higher. A link with a larger value (the value field of bigInteract, the score of BEDPE) has a thicker line. An arc with an end outside the view goes past the edge. A link to another chromosome shows as a short stub at its end in view. The arcs use the colors of the file; right-click the track and turn off Use file colors to use the track color. Put the pointer on an arc, an end or a stub to see the two ends, the distance and the other fields. A BEDPE header line gives the names of the fields. Zoom in to 50 Mb or less to see the links of a bigInteract file. A junction track shows the splice junctions of a STAR SJ.out.tab file or a junction BED file as arcs, as the junction lane of a read track does. An arc goes from the start to the end of the intron. A junction with more reads has a higher and thicker arc, with the number of its reads over it: for STAR, the uniquely mapped reads. The color shows the strand: blue for forward, vermillion for reverse, and grey when the file does not give it. Put the pointer on an arc to see the intron, the reads and the fields of the file, for STAR the multi-mapping reads, the splice motif (for example GT/AG), if the junction is annotated, and the largest overhang. In a card that you keep open, click a field to keep or hide junctions, for example the junctions with at least 10 unique reads. When more than 5,000 junctions are in view, the track shows the 5,000 with the most reads. Drag the bottom edge of the track to make it taller. A Hi-C track shows the contacts of a .hic file of Juicer (versions 6 to 9) as a triangle over the diagonal: contacts between near bins are at the bottom, and contacts between bins farther apart are higher. Each contact is a block of one bin, in rows that stand for the rotated matrix. The color goes from light grey to vermillion; the full color starts at the count that is higher than 95% of the counts in view. If the middle count in view would get less than a fifth of the full color, the colors follow a curve that gives it a fifth. This keeps a view of a whole chromosome bright, where the contacts of near bins are much higher than the others. The size of the bins follows the zoom: genie uses the smallest bin size of the file that gives blocks of 2 to 8 pixels. genie reads only the blocks of the matrix that the view needs, also from the web. Right-click a Hi-C track to select the normalization of the file, for example KR normalization or SCALE normalization, or No normalization for the counts. Without a choice, genie uses SCALE, KR, VC_SQRT or VC, in this order, if the file has it. If the file has no vector of a normalization for a chromosome at a bin size, the map shows the counts. Observed/expected divides each value by the expected value at its distance: blue below 1 and vermillion above 1, with the full colors at 1/4 and 4. Put the pointer on a block to see its two bins, their distance, the value and the normalization. Drag the bottom edge of the track to make the triangle taller. genie opens cooler files ( .cool , and .mcool with several bin sizes) as Hi-C tracks too. It reads the chromosomes, the bins and the pixels of the HDF5 file, and only the pixels of the view. The normalizations are the columns of balancing weights of the bins, such as weight normalization from cooler balance : genie multiplies each count by the weights of its two bins. Without a choice, genie uses weight if the file has it. A cooler file has no expected values, so Observed/expected divides each value by the mean value of the contacts in view at its distance. genie reads the HDF5 files that cooler writes: datasets that are whole or in chunks, with the deflate, shuffle and Fletcher-32 filters. For a virtual 4C, right-click a Hi-C track at a place and click Virtual 4C from here. A lane under the map shows the contacts of the bin at that place with each bin in view, as bars, and a line marks the place. The lane follows the normalization and Observed/expected, and the bin size follows the zoom. Put the pointer on the lane to see the value of a bin. The viewpoint must be in the loaded part of the map. Click Stop virtual 4C to remove the lane. Sessions keep the viewpoint. genie opens a table compressed with bgzip that has a tabix index as a table track, for example the CADD scores. The index gives the columns of the chromosome, the start and the end. The last header line ( #Chrom Pos … ) gives the names of the columns. A table track shows a column of numbers as a signal: at first the last column of numbers, for example PHRED. Right-click the track to show a different column, for example Show RawScore, or Show rows to see each row as a feature with its columns as fields, named by its first column of text. Zoom in to 10 Mb or less to see the data. Sessions keep the choice. A .tsv or .txt file without a tabix index stays a sample table. A GWAS track shows each variant of a file of summary statistics as a dot at the height of its -log10 p (a Manhattan plot). A grey line shows the genome-wide significance of 5×10⁻⁸, and the dots over it are vermillion. The lane goes up to the highest value in view. genie knows the file by its header line, which names the chromosome, the position and the p-value or the -log10 p, for example chromosome base_pair_location … p_value (GWAS Catalog), #CHROM POS … P (PLINK 2) or CHROM GENPOS … LOG10P (REGENIE). Put the pointer on a dot to see its row. A file with a tabix index opens at once, and genie reads only the part in view; for a file on the web, zoom in to 50 Mb or less. genie reads all of a file without an index, up to 1 GB. In the whole-genome view, every second chromosome has a lighter color. A copy number track shows the segments of each sample in a row: blue for a loss, vermillion for a gain, and light grey near 0. The full colors start at a log2 value of -1.5 and +1.5. To use a different range, right-click the track, type the minimum and the maximum, then push Enter. Default range (±1.5) goes back. genie finds the columns by the header line of the file: the sample, the chromosome, the start, the end, the number of markers and the value (for example seg.mean , log2 or MEAN_LOG2_COPY_RATIO ). If the header names no value column, genie uses the last column. A CNVkit file gets its sample name from the file name, and a GATK file from its @RG line. Up to 20 samples show expanded, with their names on the right. With more samples, the rows get thinner to fit, down to 1 px. Put the pointer on a segment to see its sample, its length, its markers and its value. Right-click the sequence to show the reverse strand and 3 or 6 reading frames. Drag a track name to move the track. Drag the bottom edge of a track to set its height. Double-click the edge to show all rows again. If a track has more than 200,000 shapes to draw in the view, it shows "There is too much to draw here. Zoom in." in place of the data.

title: Variant table
text: Right-click a variant track and click Variant table to see its variants in a table under the tracks. The palette has Show the variant table. Click the item again, or click ×, to close the table. The table has a row for each variant in view of the first locus. The columns are the chromosome, the position, the ID, the reference allele, the alternate alleles, the number of heterozygous and homozygous alternate calls (if the file has samples), Quality, Filter, the annotation fields and the INFO fields. If the track has a filter, the table shows only the variants that the filter keeps. Click a column name to sort the rows by that column: numbers in order, then text. Click again to reverse the order, and a third time to show the order of the file again. Empty cells are always last. Type in Find in the table to show only the rows with a cell that contains the text. The search ignores letter case. Click a row to go to its variant. Export TSV saves the rows in their order, with all columns, as a tab-separated file. If the view is too wide to show the variants, the table asks you to zoom in.

title: Sashimi plots
text: A Sashimi plot shows the coverage of an RNA-seq read track and the splice junctions between its exons, with the number of reads of each junction. Right-click a read track and click Sashimi plot. The track then shows the coverage as an area in the color of the track, and each splice junction as an arc with its number of reads. The first junction is above the coverage, the next one is below it, and so on, so that near arcs do not hide each other. A thicker arc has more reads. Arcs ≥ in the track menu hides the junctions with fewer reads, for example 5 or 10. To compare samples, show each read track as a Sashimi plot, give each track a different color, and turn on Shared scale in the menu of each track. The tracks then use the same range of coverage. Put the pointer on an arc to see its junction: the position, the reads, the strand and the length of the intron. To save the plots as an image, push Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on macOS), click Export… and save a PNG or an SVG file. Put a feature track with the transcripts under the read tracks to show them in the image. Click Sashimi plot again to see the reads. Sessions keep the Sashimi plot, the Arcs ≥ setting and the shared scale of each track.

title: Liftover
text: A chain file moves data from the places of one assembly to the places of a different assembly, for example from hg19 to hg38. UCSC has chain files in the liftOver folder of each genome, for example hg19ToHg38.over.chain.gz . Right-click a track and click Lift over…. Then open a chain file from the assembly of the track to the assembly in view, plain or compressed with gzip. The chain file and the data file can name the chromosomes differently, for example chr1 and 1 . genie reads only the parts of the data file that align with the view. Each feature, variant, value, link, segment and dot goes to its place in view: the span from its first to its last aligned base, on the chain that aligns the most of its bases. If that chain aligns less than half of its bases, genie does not show it. Exons and coding parts move with their feature. If the chain aligns the two assemblies on opposite strands, a feature changes its strand, and a variant shows the reverse complement of its alleles. The locus box finds the feature names and the variant IDs of a lifted track at their new places. genie cannot lift read tracks and Hi-C tracks. A lifted track does not have Next feature and Previous feature. Click Remove lift in the track menu to show the data at its own places again. Sessions keep the chain file of each track. genie reads the chain file again before it shows the track. Click Lift… under the region list to move the regions from the places of a different assembly to the places of the assembly in view, for example after you import a BED file of hg19 regions into an hg38 session. A region that the chains do not move leaves the list, and a notice gives the number. If the chains move none of the regions, the list does not change.

title: Sample groups
text: A sample table gives facts about the samples of variant and copy number tracks, for example the population, the sex or the phenotype. genie uses the table to put the rows of the samples in groups, to sort them and to color them. Open a sample table as you open a track: open the file or drop it on the window. genie reads tab or comma separated files with a header line ( .tsv , .csv , .txt , and the .panel files of the 1000 Genomes Project), IGV sample information files (the #sampleTable part) and PLINK .fam and .ped files. The column with the name sample , ID or IID has the sample names. If there is no such column, the first column has them. The other columns are the fields. In a clinical file from cBioPortal (for example data_clinical_sample.txt ), the SAMPLE_ID column has the sample names, and the fields have the names of the first line. Values such as [Not Available] count as missing. genie reads the first lines of a .txt file to know what it is, also for a file on the web. A file that starts with a hub line opens as a track hub, and a loop list ( chr1 x1 x2 chr2 y1 y2 … ) opens as an interaction track. Other .txt files open as sample tables. For a PLINK file, the fields are the family, the father, the mother, the sex (male or female) and the phenotype (affected or unaffected, or the number of a quantitative phenotype). One table applies to all tracks of the session that have its samples. A notice tells how many samples of the open tracks are in the table. Open a different table to replace it. Close the sample table in the palette removes it. Put the pointer on a genotype row or a copy number row to see the fields of its sample in the card. Click the row to keep the card open. Then click a field value, and click Group by this field, Sort by this field or Color by this field. A group shows the rows of one value together, under a band with the value and the number of samples, for example "EUR · 503 samples". Numbers come in order, then text values. A track shows at most 30 groups: the samples of the other values go together as "Other ... values". After them come the samples without a value ("No ...") and the samples that are not in the table ("Not in the sample table"). Sort puts the rows of each group in order: numbers from the smallest, text from A to Z, and samples without a value last. Color gives each row a strip at the left. The 8 most common values get 8 colors, and the other values are grey. For a field of numbers, the strip goes from light grey for the smallest number to blue for the largest. While a field groups a variant track, the card of a site shows the frequency of the other alleles (AF) in each group and the number of called alleles, for example "EUR · AF 0.12 · 1,006 alleles". genie counts two alleles for each called sample. The card shows up to 10 groups. The track menu shows the fields in use, for example Group samples by pop. Click one to stop. The palette has Group samples by, Sort samples by and Color samples by for each field and each track. If each row of a big cohort shows a group of samples, all samples of a row are in the same group.

title: Trios
text: If the sample table gives the father and the mother of a sample, and the variant track has the three samples, genie checks each variant of the child. The columns of the father and the mother can be the fields of a PLINK file, or columns with the name Father and Mother , Paternal ID and Maternal ID , or paternal_id and maternal_id . The card of a variant has the field Inheritance. Mendelian error tells that the child cannot have its call from its parents. De novo tells that the child is heterozygous and both parents are homozygous reference: the child can have a new mutation. A de novo variant is also a Mendelian error. Consistent tells that the calls agree. A variant with a missing call in a trio has no field for that trio. A frame shows around the call of a child with a Mendelian error. The card of the child's call tells the calls of the parents, for example "De novo: father homozygous reference, mother homozygous reference". The track menu has Only de novo variants and Only Mendelian errors. They add a filter on Inheritance. Then Ctrl+F and Ctrl+B go to the next and the previous variant that the filter keeps, and the variant table shows only these variants. The menu shows the filter, and you can remove it there. At a site with more than one alternate allele, a heterozygous call can have two alternate alleles. There, genie tells only the errors that no alleles can explain. A son has one X chromosome, from his mother. So genie checks X only for daughters, and it does not check Y and the mitochondria. The sex of a child comes from the PLINK sex or from a field with the name Sex or Gender (male, female, M, F, 1 or 2).

title: Sessions
text: To save the reference, the tracks (with their names, colors, ranges, overlays, sample fields and chain files), the view, the regions, the track hubs and the sample table as a session, push Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS) or click the save button. To open a session, open its .genie file. genie keeps the last session when you close it, and the start view can restore it. If a file is in the folder of the session file, the session file has its path relative to that folder.

title: Export
text: To save the view as an image, push Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on macOS) or click the camera button. The export dialog opens: Title: the title at the start of the first line of the image. Keep it empty for no title. Scale bar: a line of a round length, for example 10 kb, at the end of the first line. If the view has several loci, each panel has its own scale bar. Region bands: the regions in view (see Regions), as grey bands under the ruler. The name of a region is in its band, or next to it if the band is too short. Regions that overlap go on different rows. Push Enter or click Export…, then select the file. The session keeps the title and the two settings. The image shows the locus, the ruler and all tracks, also the tracks that are not on the screen. If the view has several loci, the image shows each panel with its locus and its ruler. In the whole-genome view, the image shows the name of each chromosome. The image uses the current theme. If the file name ends with .svg , genie saves an SVG image. The SVG has shapes and text that you can edit, for example in Inkscape or Illustrator. The text uses the fonts Inter and JetBrains Mono. If a computer does not have these fonts, it uses similar fonts. Other names give a PNG image. The scale of a PNG image is 2. Its maximum height is 16,384 px. If the view is taller, the image shows only the top part, and genie tells you.

title: Images from the command line
text: To save one image for each region in a BED file, without a window: genie snapshot work.genie regions.bed pictures The command to use depends on how you got genie: Windows: genie.exe has no console. In a terminal, use genie-cli.exe from the same folder, for example & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\genie\genie-cli.exe" snapshot work.genie regions.bed pictures in PowerShell. macOS: /Applications/genie.app/Contents/MacOS/genie snapshot work.genie regions.bed pictures . Linux: genie snapshot work.genie regions.bed pictures after you install the .deb, or ./genie-0.3.1-linux-x86_64.AppImage snapshot work.genie regions.bed pictures . Source code: cargo run -p genie -- snapshot work.genie regions.bed pictures . genie opens the session (the genome or reference, the tracks and their settings). Then it goes to each region and saves a PNG file in the folder. If the folder does not exist, genie makes it. Each image shows one region, also if the session has several loci. The name of an image is the name of the region (BED column 4) or the locus, for example chr1_1001-2000.png . If two regions have the same name, genie adds -2 , -3 and so on. The title of an image is the name of its region. For a region without a name, the title is that of the session. The scale bar and the region bands follow the session too. To set them, use the export dialog and save the session. width POINTS sets the width of the view, from 200 to 4,096 (default 1,280). A PNG image has two pixels for each point. --theme dark uses the dark theme. The default is light. --format svg saves SVG images. The default is PNG. genie writes one line for each region. If genie cannot make an image for a region, it writes the reason and continues with the next region. The exit code is 0 if genie saved all images, 1 if one or more images are missing, and 2 if the command is not correct.

title: Commands from other programs
text: While genie runs, programs on the same computer (for example R, Python or Jupyter) can control it through port 60151, as with the batch port of IGV. Send one command on each line. genie answers each line with OK or with the reason for a problem. It answers when the work is complete, for example when a new track is open and its data is loaded. Command Result genome hg38 , genome /data/genome.fa Opens a genome from the list or a reference file load /data/reads.bam name=Tumor Adds a track. name= sets the track name. goto chr1:1,000-2,000 , goto BRCA1 , goto BRCA1 BRCA2 Goes to a locus or a feature name. Two to four loci show side by side. region chr1 1001 2000 promoter Adds a region to the region list. The start and the end are 1-based and are in the region. snapshotDirectory /data/pictures Sets the folder for snapshots snapshot BRCA1.png Saves the view as an image in that folder: SVG for a name that ends with .svg , else PNG. Without a name, the image is a PNG named after the locus. expand , squish , collapse Sets the rows of all tracks, or of one track, for example squish Tumor new Removes all tracks and regions echo Answers echo import socket with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 60151)) as connection: answers = connection.makefile("r") for line in ["goto BRCA1", "snapshotDirectory /tmp", "snapshot brca1.png"]: connection.sendall((line + "\n").encode()) print(answers.readline().strip()) Put a path that has spaces between double quotes: load "/data/my reads.bam" . genie accepts maxPanelHeight and setSleepInterval , but they have no effect. Only programs on this computer can connect. genie does not answer web (HTTP) requests, so web pages cannot send commands. To close the port, open the settings and set Commands to Off. If a different program (for example IGV) uses port 60151, genie shows a message and does not take commands.

title: Settings
text: The gear button opens the settings: UI scale (90 % to 150 %), density, motion and the port for commands from other programs. genie keeps the settings and the theme in its configuration folder.

title: Updates
text: When genie starts, it asks GitHub for the newest release, at most once a day. If a newer version exists, a notice says so. Click Download to open the release page in your browser, then install the new version as usual. The check sends one request to api.github.com. The request contains the version of genie. genie sends no other data. To stop the checks at start, open the settings and set Updates to Off. Check now in the settings, Check for updates… in the genie menu and the palette always check. The settings show the version and the result of the last check, for example "genie 0.3.1 · Up to date".

title: Diagnostics
text: genie writes warnings to stderr. To see more, set GENIE_LOG to info , debug or trace : GENIE_LOG=debug cargo run -p genie In a debug build, F12 shows the time of each update and view, the frame time and the use of the caches.

title: Test
text: cargo test --workspace The tests give cut and damaged copies of each test file to the readers: 3 copies of each file. Each reader must give an error or data, and must not panic or hang. The full sweep makes about 24 copies of each file and takes a few minutes: cargo test -p genie --bin genie sweep -- --ignored

title: Website
text: The project page in docs/ comes from the pages in site/ , this README (the manual), the changelog, the keys of genie and its logo. A test fails when a file in docs/ is out of date. To write the files again: GENIE_WRITE_SITE=1 cargo test -p genie --bin genie site The clips of the tutorial and the pictures are files in docs/clips/ and docs/images/ . To record the clips again after a change of the look, run this PowerShell script ( pwsh on macOS and Linux). It needs ffmpeg with libx264 and libwebp: powershell -File site/clips/record.ps1 genie runs without a window, and a script in crates/genie/src/app/clips.rs moves the pointer and clicks. The clips use real data from the web: a first run of all clips fetches about 35 MB. The work folder target/clips keeps the fetched ranges, so a later run fetches only new ranges. -Clips cards, hero records some of the clips, -Cap 60MB changes the most bytes that all runs can fetch (50 MB), and -SkipRecord encodes the frames of the last run again.
